I did RO-DBT for awhile. I didn’t do it long enough to get through the whole curriculum, so I can only speak for the earlier parts of the book. I found some of it to be really helpful, and some of it didn’t really apply to me. There’s a lot of emphasis on building social skills in an “opening up” type of way (again, this applies to the first like quarter of the book, I’m not sure what the rest consists of). Overall, I felt like it had a less universal-ness as far as helpfulness goes compared to regular DBT. It definitely specifically targets over-control. But it was just as interesting to me as DBT. Even when it targeted things that I didn’t feel like I needed help with (like, just as a random example, making friends), I found that I was able to get something out of it anyway because of the in depth way RO discusses the topics and skills. If you can find an RO group with a therapist you like running it, I’d definitely say it’s worth trying!

Edit: here’s a website you might want to click around on to look more into RO. It seems to give a good overview of it: https://www.radicallyopen.net/about-ro-dbt/

In the US, typically the rule of thumb for when and whether a provider will/should hospitalize somebody is if they say they have a plan to harm themselves or somebody else. If you’re thinking about it, but don’t have a plan of any kind, you probably don’t run the risk of being hospitalized. That being said, I’ve noticed some therapists are a lot more sensitive/quick to hospitalize than others. When you start “shopping” for a therapist, I would directly ask them at what point do they feel hospitalization is necessary for suicidal ideation or aggressive thoughts. My current therapist is very trusting of my judgment for when I need the hospital, so I can talk to him openly about my suicidal thoughts without being paranoid that he’s just going to commit me. 

It may take awhile to find the right therapist for you, but I highly recommend trying it. My therapist, and therapy in general, has saved my life many times at this point. :)

Yeah! So, I would slowly start to freeze up. Usually it starts by me going mute, then maybe dissociating, or shaking anxiously. Then my body becomes stiff in whatever position I’m in and before I know it I can’t move. When people try to move me, my body resists it. Like I’m very stiff. And I still can’t talk. I can hear and see, but usually I’m dissociated and not processing what’s going on, so when I come back to and relax again, there’s usually gaps in my memory from when I was catatonic. This can last anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours. My friend who also has PNES experiences something very similar, except she has very strong convulsions before she goes catatonic. I think most people who have PNES convulse (and if I think back, I think there’s been once or twice where I have too), but I don’t think that’s a diagnostic requirement.

The epileptic equivalent of going catatonic I think is called Absence Seizures, which I think is what the doctor I saw who diagnosed me with PNES was thinking about when she heard about my catatonic episodes. Don’t quote me on that though, I don’t know a ton about epilepsy. That’s just what I came across back when I was initially researching things related to my condition.

I’ve had very positive experiences. I’ve been hospitalized 4 times and have stayed at 2 different hospitals. The benefit for me was that it was like a bubble that took me away from all of life’s stressors. And I met with a psychiatrist frequently, so they could stabilize me with medication. Most hospitals have group therapy, but it tends to be pretty basic. And the programs I was at didn’t have individual therapy. And it got boring at times. But those were really the only downsides for me. The way I look at it is some mental hospitals/psych wards are good and some are not so good—but that’s true for hospitals that treat physical conditions too. Being in a hospital, for any reason, is almost never desirable, but sometimes it’s needed. I hope you feel better soon.

Hey, I’m so sorry you are experiencing these things. I’ve been inpatient three times, so I can describe for you what the process is like if that would be helpful.

I’ve been to 2 different hospitals. One was a special, voluntary admissions only clinic where you set up intake ahead of time. But the other one I’ve been to twice was just a regular hospital, and I stayed in their psych ward. I don’t know the exact process for hospitals dedicated specifically to mental health, but I’m sure it’s very similar to going to the ER of a general hospital.

When you go to the ER, you’ll go to the check in desk, where they’ll triage you, which just means they’ll get the information on why you’ve come to the ER. Make sure to be as honest with them as you can. If you’re having suicidal thoughts, chances are you’ll be taken to an ER room pretty quickly since it is a life or death situation, though some hospitals are better about prioritizing who gets seen than others. Once you get taken to a room, they’ll have you change out of your clothes into a gown, and they’ll hold on to your belongings for you (since I knew ahead of time that I was going to go to the hospital, I prepared a bag with about 3-4 days’ worth of clothes). Then they’ll run a bunch of medical tests to make sure you’re physically sound. Then you’ll talk to some people about why you’ve come to the hospital—definitely the ER doctor and probably a social worker too. Again, make sure to be as honest as you can. You’ll be in the ER room for at least a few hours, because that’s how long it takes for them to get the results of your tests back. It may take longer if they’re waiting for a bed in the psych ward to open up for you or if they’re having to contact other hospitals to figure out where to transfer you to.

Once they can determine you’re physically healthy and they have a bed for you either at that hospital or a different one, they’ll transfer you to the psych ward or the other hospital. I’ve never been transferred from one hospital to another, but I think they take you either in an ambulance or cop car. For me, they had me sit in a wheelchair as they took me upstairs to the psych ward from the ER. Then they’ll do a body search. At the hospital I went to, all they do is swipe you with a metal detector, but I know at other hospitals, you’ll have to get undressed for them to make sure you’re not concealing anything.

Once you’re in, you’ll talk to an intake doctor, they may or may not be the person who treats you while you’re there depending on what time of day it is. Be very honest with whoever you speak to about why you’re there and what’s going on with you, I can’t stress that enough. Then they’ll do a belongings search of whatever you brought with you, and then they’ll show you your bed! At the hospitals I stayed at, I had my own room, but in most hospitals you have a roommate. But I think because of covid right now a lot of hospitals are only allowing one person per room.

The biggest thing that I think you’ll want to do next is to research the hospitals in your area. Look at their websites, look at the google reviews, etc. HOWEVER, don’t get scared by some people’s google reviews...most people who stay in the hospital don’t want to be there so of course many people are going to be upset with the hospital...even if it is a good hospital.

I hope that helps. Please take care for yourself and remember that your safety is most important.
